# k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN)

::: {.callout-note title="Connection with the theoretical volume"}
The mathematical foundations of distances, scaling, and nearest-neighbor methods are developed in greater depth in Chapters 2 and 12 of *Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning* [@rodriguez2026fundamentos].
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter, the reader will be able to:

- explain the classification logic of k-NN;
- calculate and interpret Euclidean distance;
- prepare numerical and categorical predictors for distance-based classification;
- avoid information leakage during scaling;
- create stratified training, validation, and test partitions;
- choose $k$ using validation while preserving the test set for final evaluation;
- interpret accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and balanced accuracy;
- recognize the effects of class imbalance and high dimensionality on k-NN.

## Core idea

k-NN (*k-nearest neighbors*) classifies a new observation according to the most common class among its $k$ nearest neighbors [@fix1951discriminatory; @cover1967nearest]. It is often described as a **lazy learner** because it does not estimate a parametric prediction equation during training; much of the computation takes place when a new observation is classified.

```{r knn-intuitive-example-en, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
library(ggplot2)
library(class)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
source("../util_graficas.R")

example_data <- data.frame(
  hour = c(8, 9, 10, 18, 19, 20, 22, 23),
  month = c(1, 1, 2, 6, 6, 7, 12, 12),
  class = c(
    "Property damage only", "Property damage only", "Property damage only",
    "With casualties", "With casualties", "With casualties",
    "With casualties", "With casualties"
  )
)

ggplot(example_data, aes(x = hour, y = month, color = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  escala_clases_color() +
  labs(
    title = "Intuitive k-NN example",
    subtitle = "Classification depends on the nearest observations",
    x = "Hour",
    y = "Month",
    color = "Class"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

## Euclidean distance

For two points in two dimensions,

$$
d(A,B)=\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2}.
$$

With $p$ predictors,

$$
d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=
\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p}(x_j-x'_j)^2}.
$$

```{r knn-distance-en}
sqrt((8 - 10)^2 + (1 - 2)^2)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Interpretation"}
A smaller distance indicates greater proximity in predictor space. That proximity is meaningful only when variables have been represented and scaled appropriately.
:::

## Why scaling matters

If one variable ranges from 0 to 1000 and another from 0 to 1, the first can dominate Euclidean distance even when it is not substantively more important. A continuous predictor can be standardized as

$$
z_{ij}=\frac{x_{ij}-\bar{x}_{j,\text{train}}}{s_{j,\text{train}}}.
$$

::: {.callout-important title="Avoiding information leakage"}
The means and standard deviations used to transform validation and test observations must be estimated **only from training data**. Scaling with the complete dataset would leak test information into model construction.
:::

In this chapter, categorical predictors are converted to 0/1 indicator variables with `model.matrix()`. The continuous hour variable is standardized, while binary indicators remain 0/1. Standardizing rare indicator columns can unintentionally give uncommon categories excessive weight because their standard deviations are very small.

## Helper functions for rigorous evaluation

```{r knn-helper-functions-en}
stratified_split <- function(y, prop_train = 0.60, prop_val = 0.20, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  y <- factor(y)

  idx_train <- integer(0)
  idx_val <- integer(0)
  idx_test <- integer(0)

  for (class_value in levels(y)) {
    ids <- sample(which(y == class_value))
    n_train <- floor(prop_train * length(ids))
    n_val <- floor(prop_val * length(ids))

    ids_train <- ids[seq_len(n_train)]
    remaining <- ids[-seq_len(n_train)]
    ids_val <- remaining[seq_len(n_val)]
    ids_test <- setdiff(remaining, ids_val)

    idx_train <- c(idx_train, ids_train)
    idx_val <- c(idx_val, ids_val)
    idx_test <- c(idx_test, ids_test)
  }

  list(
    train = sort(idx_train),
    validation = sort(idx_val),
    test = sort(idx_test)
  )
}

binary_metrics <- function(actual, predicted, positive, negative) {
  actual <- factor(actual, levels = c(positive, negative))
  predicted <- factor(predicted, levels = c(positive, negative))
  m <- table(Actual = actual, Predicted = predicted)

  TP <- m[positive, positive]
  FN <- m[positive, negative]
  FP <- m[negative, positive]
  TN <- m[negative, negative]

  safe_divide <- function(a, b) if (b == 0) NA_real_ else a / b

  sensitivity <- safe_divide(TP, TP + FN)
  specificity <- safe_divide(TN, TN + FP)

  data.frame(
    accuracy = safe_divide(TP + TN, sum(m)),
    sensitivity = sensitivity,
    specificity = specificity,
    balanced_accuracy = mean(c(sensitivity, specificity), na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}
```

# Applied Case A: ATUS

## Load and prepare the dataset

To keep computation manageable, we use a reproducible sample of up to 12,000 traffic accidents. The sample is intended to teach the algorithm rather than replace a full analysis of the complete ATUS dataset.

```{r load-prepare-knn-atus-en}
atus_path <- "../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv"

if (!file.exists(atus_path)) {
  stop("../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv was not found. Run Chapter 2 first.")
}

atus_ml <- read_csv(atus_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

set.seed(2026)
atus_knn_base <- atus_ml |>
  mutate(
    accident_class = factor(
      accidente_con_victimas,
      levels = c("Con víctimas", "Solo daños"),
      labels = c("With casualties", "Property damage only")
    ),
    MES = as.factor(MES),
    HOUR_NUM = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(ID_HORA)),
    HOUR_NUM = ifelse(
      HOUR_NUM >= 0 & HOUR_NUM <= 23,
      HOUR_NUM,
      NA_real_
    ),
    DIASEMANA = as.factor(DIASEMANA),
    TIPACCID = as.factor(TIPACCID),
    CAUSAACCI = as.factor(CAUSAACCI)
  ) |>
  drop_na(
    accident_class,
    MES,
    HOUR_NUM,
    DIASEMANA,
    TIPACCID,
    CAUSAACCI
  ) |>
  slice_sample(n = min(12000, n()))

prop.table(table(atus_knn_base$accident_class))
```

## Build the predictor matrix

```{r knn-predictor-matrix-en}
predictor_matrix <- model.matrix(
  ~ HOUR_NUM + MES + DIASEMANA + TIPACCID + CAUSAACCI - 1,
  data = atus_knn_base
)

y_atus <- atus_knn_base$accident_class

dim(predictor_matrix)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Dummy variables and dimensionality"}
Each categorical predictor produces several indicator columns. This increases the dimensionality of the space. In high dimensions, distances tend to become more similar and truly close neighbors can be harder to distinguish; this is one aspect of the **curse of dimensionality**.
:::

## Training, validation, and test sets

```{r knn-split-atus-en}
parts_atus <- stratified_split(
  y_atus,
  prop_train = 0.60,
  prop_val = 0.20,
  seed = 2026
)

x_train <- predictor_matrix[parts_atus$train, , drop = FALSE]
x_val <- predictor_matrix[parts_atus$validation, , drop = FALSE]
x_test <- predictor_matrix[parts_atus$test, , drop = FALSE]

y_train <- y_atus[parts_atus$train]
y_val <- y_atus[parts_atus$validation]
y_test <- y_atus[parts_atus$test]

rbind(
  training = prop.table(table(y_train)),
  validation = prop.table(table(y_val)),
  test = prop.table(table(y_test))
)
```

## Scale the continuous predictor using training data

```{r knn-scaling-atus-en}
mean_hour <- mean(x_train[, "HOUR_NUM"])
sd_hour <- sd(x_train[, "HOUR_NUM"])
if (sd_hour == 0) sd_hour <- 1

x_train_z <- x_train
x_val_z <- x_val
x_test_z <- x_test

x_train_z[, "HOUR_NUM"] <-
  (x_train[, "HOUR_NUM"] - mean_hour) / sd_hour
x_val_z[, "HOUR_NUM"] <-
  (x_val[, "HOUR_NUM"] - mean_hour) / sd_hour
x_test_z[, "HOUR_NUM"] <-
  (x_test[, "HOUR_NUM"] - mean_hour) / sd_hour
```

## Select k using validation data

The test set should not be used to tune hyperparameters. We compare several odd values of $k$ on the **validation set** and select the value with the largest balanced accuracy.

```{r select-k-atus-en}
k_values <- c(3, 5, 7, 11, 15, 21)

validation_results <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(k_values, function(current_k) {
    pred <- knn(
      train = x_train_z,
      test = x_val_z,
      cl = y_train,
      k = current_k
    )

    m <- binary_metrics(
      y_val,
      pred,
      positive = "With casualties",
      negative = "Property damage only"
    )
    m$k <- current_k
    m
  })
) |>
  select(k, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, balanced_accuracy)

validation_results

best_k <- validation_results$k[
  which.max(validation_results$balanced_accuracy)
]

best_k
```

```{r plot-k-selection-atus-en, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.8}
validation_long <- validation_results |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, balanced_accuracy),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  )

ggplot(
  validation_long,
  aes(x = k, y = value, color = metric, group = metric)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      accuracy = col_azul,
      sensitivity = col_coral,
      specificity = col_turquesa,
      balanced_accuracy = col_morado
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Selecting k on the validation set",
    subtitle = "The test set remains untouched until final evaluation",
    x = "k",
    y = "Metric value",
    color = "Metric"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

## Final evaluation on the test set

After $k$ has been selected, training and validation observations are combined as the reference set and the model is evaluated **once** on the test data.

```{r final-knn-evaluation-atus-en}
x_reference <- rbind(x_train_z, x_val_z)
y_reference <- factor(
  c(as.character(y_train), as.character(y_val)),
  levels = levels(y_atus)
)

pred_test_atus <- knn(
  train = x_reference,
  test = x_test_z,
  cl = y_reference,
  k = best_k
)

confusion_test_atus <- table(
  Actual = factor(y_test, levels = c("With casualties", "Property damage only")),
  Predicted = factor(pred_test_atus, levels = c("With casualties", "Property damage only"))
)

confusion_test_atus

binary_metrics(
  y_test,
  pred_test_atus,
  positive = "With casualties",
  negative = "Property damage only"
)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Why balanced accuracy?"}
When one class is much more frequent, overall accuracy can favor the majority group. Balanced accuracy averages sensitivity and specificity, giving equal importance to both classes.
:::

# Interactive laboratory: k-NN

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Choose the number of neighbors and move a new observation. The laboratory highlights the points that participate in the decision and shows their votes.

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 760
#| components: [viewer]

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("k-NN classification laboratory"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("k", "Number of neighbors k", 1, 15, 5, step = 2),
      sliderInput("xnew", "Sepal length", 4, 8, 5.8, step = 0.1),
      sliderInput("ynew", "Sepal width", 2, 4.5, 3.0, step = 0.1)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("plot", height = "500px"),
      verbatimTextOutput("result"),
      textOutput("explanation")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  result <- reactive({
    X <- as.matrix(iris[, c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width")])
    new_point <- c(input$xnew, input$ynew)

    distances <- sqrt(rowSums(sweep(X, 2, new_point, "-")^2))
    indices <- order(distances)[seq_len(input$k)]
    votes <- table(iris$Species[indices])
    predicted_class <- names(which.max(votes))

    list(indices = indices, votes = votes, class = predicted_class)
  })

  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    r <- result()
    species_code <- as.integer(iris$Species)

    plot(
      iris$Sepal.Length,
      iris$Sepal.Width,
      pch = 19,
      col = species_code,
      xlab = "Sepal length",
      ylab = "Sepal width",
      main = paste("Prediction:", r$class)
    )

    points(
      iris$Sepal.Length[r$indices],
      iris$Sepal.Width[r$indices],
      pch = 1,
      cex = 2.1,
      lwd = 2
    )

    points(input$xnew, input$ynew, pch = 8, cex = 2.2, lwd = 3)

    segments(
      input$xnew,
      input$ynew,
      iris$Sepal.Length[r$indices],
      iris$Sepal.Width[r$indices],
      lty = 3
    )

    legend(
      "topright",
      legend = levels(iris$Species),
      col = seq_along(levels(iris$Species)),
      pch = 19,
      bty = "n"
    )
  })

  output$result <- renderPrint({
    r <- result()
    cat("Predicted class:", r$class, "\n\n")
    cat("Neighbor votes:\n")
    print(r$votes)
  })

  output$explanation <- renderText({
    paste0(
      "The large circles identify the ", input$k,
      " neighbors used in the vote. The star is the new observation."
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
:::

# Applied Case B: k-NN with COVID-19

We use the same reproducible period-selection rule introduced in Chapters 2, 3, and 5. The objective is to classify the administrative outcome `MURIO` strictly for teaching purposes.

```{r select-covid-period-knn-en}
covid_counts <- read_csv(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados/conteo_casos_confirmados_2020_2025.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

covid_year <- covid_counts |>
  filter(ESTADO == "PROCESADO", !is.na(CASOS_CONFIRMADOS)) |>
  slice_max(CASOS_CONFIRMADOS, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  pull(ANIO)

covid_path <- file.path(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados",
  paste0("covid19_mexico_", covid_year, "_ml_preparado.csv.gz")
)

if (!file.exists(covid_path)) {
  stop("The COVID-19 dataset selected by the reproducible procedure was not found.")
}

message("COVID-19 period used: ", covid_year)
```

## Prepare an educational sample

```{r prepare-covid-knn-en}
covid_knn <- read_csv(covid_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(
    MURIO,
    EDAD,
    NEUMONIA,
    DIABETES,
    HIPERTENSION,
    OBESIDAD,
    RENAL_CRONICA,
    NUM_COMORBILIDADES
  ) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    outcome = factor(
      MURIO,
      levels = c(1, 0),
      labels = c("Recorded death", "No recorded death")
    )
  ) |>
  select(-MURIO)

set.seed(2026)
covid_knn <- covid_knn |>
  slice_sample(n = min(12000, n()))

X_covid <- covid_knn |>
  select(-outcome) |>
  as.matrix()
y_covid <- covid_knn$outcome
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Educational use only"}
This exercise illustrates k-NN behavior. It is not a clinical calculator, diagnostic instrument, or validated prognostic model. If the educational sample changes class prevalence, its proportions also do not represent population rates.
:::

## COVID-19 partition and scaling

`EDAD` and `NUM_COMORBILIDADES` are continuous or count predictors and are standardized. Binary clinical indicators remain coded 0/1.

```{r covid-knn-split-scale-en}
parts_covid <- stratified_split(
  y_covid,
  prop_train = 0.60,
  prop_val = 0.20,
  seed = 2026
)

xc_train <- X_covid[parts_covid$train, , drop = FALSE]
xc_val <- X_covid[parts_covid$validation, , drop = FALSE]
xc_test <- X_covid[parts_covid$test, , drop = FALSE]

yc_train <- y_covid[parts_covid$train]
yc_val <- y_covid[parts_covid$validation]
yc_test <- y_covid[parts_covid$test]

continuous_vars <- intersect(c("EDAD", "NUM_COMORBILIDADES"), colnames(xc_train))

xc_train_z <- xc_train
xc_val_z <- xc_val
xc_test_z <- xc_test

for (variable in continuous_vars) {
  mean_value <- mean(xc_train[, variable])
  sd_value <- sd(xc_train[, variable])
  if (sd_value == 0) sd_value <- 1

  xc_train_z[, variable] <- (xc_train[, variable] - mean_value) / sd_value
  xc_val_z[, variable] <- (xc_val[, variable] - mean_value) / sd_value
  xc_test_z[, variable] <- (xc_test[, variable] - mean_value) / sd_value
}
```

## Select k and evaluate once on the test set

```{r select-k-covid-en}
k_values_covid <- c(3, 5, 7, 11, 15, 21)

covid_validation_results <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(k_values_covid, function(current_k) {
    p <- knn(xc_train_z, xc_val_z, yc_train, k = current_k)
    m <- binary_metrics(
      yc_val,
      p,
      positive = "Recorded death",
      negative = "No recorded death"
    )
    m$k <- current_k
    m
  })
) |>
  select(k, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, balanced_accuracy)

covid_validation_results

best_k_covid <- covid_validation_results$k[
  which.max(covid_validation_results$balanced_accuracy)
]

best_k_covid
```

```{r final-covid-knn-evaluation-en}
xc_reference <- rbind(xc_train_z, xc_val_z)
yc_reference <- factor(
  c(as.character(yc_train), as.character(yc_val)),
  levels = levels(y_covid)
)

pred_covid_test <- knn(
  train = xc_reference,
  test = xc_test_z,
  cl = yc_reference,
  k = best_k_covid
)

confusion_covid_knn <- table(
  Actual = factor(yc_test, levels = c("Recorded death", "No recorded death")),
  Predicted = factor(pred_covid_test, levels = c("Recorded death", "No recorded death"))
)

confusion_covid_knn

binary_metrics(
  yc_test,
  pred_covid_test,
  positive = "Recorded death",
  negative = "No recorded death"
)
```

## Interpreting k

Small values of $k$ produce highly local decision boundaries and can react strongly to noise. Larger values smooth the rule and may erase local structure. The appropriate value depends on the data and should be chosen with validation or cross-validation, **not by repeatedly optimizing performance on the final test set**.

## Chapter summary

k-NN is easy to explain, but reliable use requires disciplined preprocessing: meaningful variable representation, leakage-free scaling, proper data partitioning, and selection of $k$ away from the final test set. Performance can also deteriorate with high dimensionality or strong class imbalance, so validation design and class-sensitive metrics are essential parts of the method.
